p1: Cut the tenderloin into medallions or strips and pat them very dry; season with salt and pepper.
Heat the oil and brown the sliced garlic over medium heat without burning it. Lift it out and set aside.
Turn the heat to maximum and sear the beef in batches, never crowding the pan.
Return the garlic, toss for 30 seconds and serve at once.
High heat and a roomy pan are everything: crowd the beef and it steams instead of browning.
p2: Cut the beef into thin strips against the grain and season.
Sear the beef over high heat in the oil, then lift it out of the pan.
In the same fat, soften onion, garlic and tomato until they break down.
Return the beef, toss and cook 2 minutes more to bring the flavours together.
Sear the beef first and take it out: leave it in while the sofrito cooks and it turns tough.
p3: Cut the potato into batons and fry until golden; set aside.
Cut the beef into thick strips and sear over very high heat.
Add the onion in wedges and the tomato in segments; toss without letting them collapse.
Pour in the soy and vinegar, let it steam off and fold in the potatoes.
The vegetables should stay crisp, not soft: three minutes in the pan and out.
p4: Soften the chopped onion and garlic until translucent.
Add the beef and brown it well, breaking up the lumps with a spoon.
Stir in the chopped tomato and cook until it melts down.
Adjust salt and spices; let it reduce until no loose liquid remains.
Brown the beef properly before the tomato goes in: that is where the flavour is built.
p5: Mix the beef with the egg, soaked bread, chopped garlic and salt; roll into balls.
Brown the meatballs on the outside in the oil and lift them out.
In the same pan soften onion and garlic, add the tomato and season.
Return the meatballs and simmer gently until the sauce thickens.
Do not cook them through while browning: they finish inside the sauce and stay juicy.
p6: Sear the cubed beef on every side in the butter.
Soften onion, garlic and carrot in the same pot.
Pour in the wine and reduce it by half to cook off the alcohol.
Add the stock, cover and simmer gently until the beef is tender.
Always reduce the wine before the stock goes in, or the sauce stays sharp and acidic.
p7: Joint the chicken into small pieces and season well.
Brown the sliced garlic in the oil and set it aside.
Brown the chicken over medium-high heat on every side.
Return the garlic, cover and finish over low heat.
Small pieces cook evenly and come out golden outside and juicy inside.
p8: Butterfly the breast or flatten it to an even thickness.
Marinate with lime, oil, salt and pepper; rest 10 min.
Cook in a properly hot pan for 4 minutes a side without moving it.
Even thickness is everything: if one side is thick, the thin side dries out waiting for it.
p9: Sear the chicken pieces in the oil until golden.
Add onion, garlic and tomato; cook until they form the braise.
Add the potato in chunks and water or stock to come halfway up.
Cover and simmer gently until everything is tender.
Searing the chicken first leaves golden fond in the pot: that is where the braise gets its flavour.
p10: Soften onion and garlic until lightly golden.
Add the cubed chicken and seal it on the outside.
Stir in the curry and toast it for 1 minute to release the aroma.
Pour in the coconut milk and simmer gently until it thickens.
Toasting the spice in fat before any liquid multiplies the flavour. It is called blooming.
p11: Flatten the breasts and season them.
Pass each one through flour, then beaten egg, then breadcrumbs.
Fry in medium-hot oil until golden on both sides.
Drain on a rack or paper so the crust does not go soft.
Flour then egg then crumb is not fussiness: the flour dries the surface so the coating grips.
p12: Marinate the chicken with crushed garlic, lime, oil, salt and oregano.
Cut the potatoes into wedges and lay them in the tray as a bed.
Set the chicken on top and roast at 200°C.
Raise to 220°C for the last few minutes to crisp the skin.
The potatoes underneath drink up the chicken juices. They are the best part of the dish.
p13: Season the wings and roast at 200°C until golden.
Mix honey, soy, mustard and grated garlic for the glaze.
Brush the wings and return them to the oven to caramelize.
Brush once more for a glossy coat.
Never glaze at the start: the sugar burns long before the chicken is cooked.
p14: Cut the pork into cubes and sear over high heat.
Lift it out and toss the pepper and onion, keeping them crisp.
Mix soy, vinegar and sugar; pour it in and let it bubble.
Return the pork and glaze until the sauce coats it.
The sweet-sour balance is set at the end: taste and correct with more vinegar or sugar.
p15: Take the meat out of the fridge 20 minutes ahead and season it.
Sear in a very hot pan for 3 minutes a side.
Lower the heat, add garlic and butter and spoon the fat over the meat.
Lift out and rest 5 minutes before slicing.
Spooning the butter over at the end (basting) adds flavour and finishes the cooking gently.
p16: Lay the bacon in a COLD pan, with no oil.
Turn the heat to medium-low and let it render its own fat.
Turn it once golden and finish the other side.
Drain on paper; it crisps as it cools.
Starting in a cold pan is the trick: the fat melts slowly and it cooks evenly instead of burnt outside and raw inside.
p17: Slice the potato thin and cut the onion into wedges.
Confit them in oil over low heat until soft, without colouring. Drain.
Beat the eggs with salt and fold in the potato; rest 5 min.
Set it in a pan with a little oil and flip it using a plate.
The potato is confited, not fried: it must stay pale and soft for the tortilla to be creamy.
p18: Sauté the sliced mushrooms over high heat until golden.
Add the chopped garlic and toss for 30 seconds.
Lower the heat, pour in the beaten eggs and stir slowly.
Pull them off while still creamy: they keep cooking off the heat.
Mushrooms on high heat and no salt at the start: salt draws out water and they steam instead of browning.
p19: Beat the eggs with salt until smooth, without whipping in air.
Wilt the spinach in the butter and set it aside.
Pour the egg into a pan over medium-low heat and draw the edges inward.
When it is almost set, add the filling and fold it in half.
Medium-low heat: a French omelette should not colour, it stays pale and tender.
p20: Soften onion, garlic and tomato until they form a sauce.
Blend or crush the sauce and return it to the pan.
Make wells in the sauce and crack the eggs into them.
Cover and cook until the white sets and the yolk stays runny.
Covering the pan sets the white from above without drying the yolk.
p21: Bring a generously salted pot of water to the boil for the pasta.
Brown the garlic in the oil over low heat without burning it.
Add the tomato and cook until the sharpness is gone.
Toss the al dente pasta with the sauce and a splash of the cooking water.
Always keep a cup of the cooking water: the starch is what binds the sauce to the strands.
p22: Cook the pasta in salted water; reserve a cup of the water.
Crisp the bacon strips in their own fat.
Beat the yolks with the grated cheese and plenty of pepper.
Off the heat, toss the hot pasta with the egg, loosening with water.
Carbonara has no cream: the creaminess comes from emulsified egg. And always off the heat, or it scrambles.
p23: Sauté the mushrooms over high heat until well browned.
Add garlic, then the cream, and let it reduce a little.
Toss with the pasta and loosen with cooking water.
Brown the mushrooms in batches if there are many: crowded, they release water and never brown.
p24: Cook the pasta in salted water.
Soften the garlic in oil and add the chopped tomato.
Fold in the drained tuna and warm it without breaking it up completely.
Toss with the pasta and finish with fresh parsley.
Add the tuna at the end: cook it long and it dries out and turns chalky.
p25: Toast the rice in the oil for a minute to seal the grain.
Add the hot water or stock and the salt; boil uncovered.
When craters appear on the surface, drop the heat to minimum and cover.
Cook covered without lifting the lid; turn off and rest 5 min.
Golden rule: do not lift the lid. The trapped steam is what finishes cooking the grain.
p26: Use cold, loose rice cooked the day before.
Scramble the egg in the pan and set it aside.
Toss the diced carrot and peas over high heat.
Add the rice, soy and egg; keep everything moving.
Day-old rice, never fresh: hot damp rice clumps and turns to mush.
p27: Sear the shrimp for 1 minute a side and lift them out.
Soften onion, garlic, tomato and pepper in the same pot.
Add the rice, stir, and pour in the hot stock.
Cook covered and return the shrimp for the last 3 minutes.
Shrimp need only 2-3 minutes. Cook them with the rice from the start and they turn rubbery.
p28: Keep the stock hot in a second pot; this matters.
Soften the onion, add the rice and toast it for 2 minutes.
Add hot stock a ladle at a time, stirring, waiting for each to absorb.
Off the heat, beat in cold butter and cheese until creamy.
The stock must ALWAYS be hot: cold stock stops the cooking and the grain opens badly.
p29: Soften onion and garlic in the pot until translucent.
Add the hard vegetables (potato, carrot) and toss for 2 minutes.
Pour in the stock and simmer over medium heat.
Add the soft vegetables at the end so they hold their shape.
Hard vegetables first, soft ones after: that way everything finishes at its point together.
p30: Soften onion and garlic until lightly golden.
Add the chopped tomato and cook until it collapses.
Pour in the stock, boil and blend until very smooth.
Return to the pot, stir in the cream and adjust the salt.
A pinch of sugar corrects the tomato's acidity without making it taste sweet.
p31: Soften onion and garlic in the butter.
Add the diced potato and the stock; cook until tender.
Add the spinach and cook only 2 minutes to keep the colour.
Blend, return to the pot and finish with cream.
Spinach last and briefly: boil it and the bright green is gone.
p32: Soften onion, garlic, carrot and tomato for the base.
Add the washed lentils and stir.
Pour in the stock and cook over medium heat until tender.
Season with salt at the end and adjust the thickness.
Salt the lentils at the end: early salt can toughen the skin of the grain.
p33: Put the meat in cold water and bring to the boil; skim off the foam.
Add spring onion, garlic and salt; simmer gently.
Add the whole potato and cook until tender.
Serve with chopped fresh cilantro on top.
Start in cold water and skim: that is what keeps the broth clear instead of cloudy.
p34: Build a sofrito with onion, garlic and tomato.
Add the chopped ripe plantain and let it melt down.
Fold in the cooked beans with some of their liquid.
Simmer gently until thick and bound.
The dissolved ripe plantain is what gives paisa beans their sweetness and thick body.
p35: Brown the sliced chorizo and set it aside; keep the fat.
Soften onion, garlic and carrot in that fat.
Add the lentils and stock; cook until tender.
Return the chorizo for the last few minutes.
The fat the chorizo releases is the best base you will get for the sofrito. Do not throw it out.
p36: Drain and dry the cooked chickpeas thoroughly.
Brown the sliced garlic and the onion in the oil.
Add the chickpeas and toss until they take on a little colour.
Dust the paprika in off the heat so it does not burn.
Ground spices burn in seconds: add them at the end or off the heat.
p37: Boil the peeled potatoes in salted water until very soft.
Drain and let them dry for a minute over the heat to lose moisture.
Mash them hot and work in the butter first.
Add the warm milk little by little to the texture you want.
Butter before milk: the fat coats the starch and stops the mash turning gluey.
p38: Cut the potatoes into even wedges and dry them very well.
Toss with oil, salt and spices until every piece is coated.
Spread in a single layer, never overlapping, on the tray.
No crowding and properly dry: moisture makes steam, and steam stops them browning.
p39: Cut every vegetable to the same size before you light the heat.
Heat the pan until it lightly smokes.
Toss the hard ones first (carrot, broccoli), moving constantly.
Add the soft ones, the garlic and the soy; toss 2 minutes more.
In a wok everything is cut beforehand: once you start there is no time to chop anything.
p40: Cut the broccoli into florets and blanch 3 min in boiling salted water.
Move it straight into cold water to lock in the green.
Brown the sliced garlic in the oil over medium heat.
Toss the drained broccoli and finish with lime.
The cold-water shock is what keeps the green so intense.
p41: Slit the plantain lengthways without cutting through, skin on.
Rub it with butter and bake at 200°C until very soft.
Open the slit and fill it with the cheese.
Return to the oven until the cheese melts.
The blacker the skin, the sweeter the result. Do not use firm yellow plantain.
p42: Mash the avocado with a fork, leaving some texture.
Add the lime straight away so it does not oxidize.
Fold in finely chopped onion and tomato.
Season with salt and cilantro to taste.
Lime first, not last: it is the only thing stopping it from turning brown.
p43: Cut the tomato and avocado into even wedges.
Soak the sliced onion in cold water for 5 min to take off the bite.
Mix oil, lime and salt for the dressing.
Dress it right before serving so it does not weep.
Dress at the last moment: salt pulls water out of the tomato and waters down the salad if you wait.
p44: Mix vinegar, mustard, salt and pepper in a bowl.
Add the oil in a thin stream while whisking without stopping.
Keep going until it thickens and comes together.
Keep in a jar; shake before using.
Classic ratio: three parts oil to one of vinegar. The mustard is the emulsifier that holds them together.
p45: Dry the fish very well and season it just before cooking.
Heat the pan with oil until properly hot.
Cook the skin side first, pressing down, without moving it.
Turn once only and finish with garlic, lime and butter.
Turn it once. Move it around more than that and the fish falls apart.
p46: Marinate the fish with lime and salt; rest 10 min.
Soften onion, garlic and tomato to build the base.
Pour in the coconut milk and let it reduce a little.
Add the fish and cook gently, without stirring.
Do not stir: move the pan instead of using a spoon, and the fish stays whole.
p47: Heat the oil with the sliced garlic over medium heat.
Raise the heat, add the shrimp and toss for 1 minute a side.
Pull them off as soon as they turn pink; finish with parsley.
When the shrimp curls into a C it is ready; if it curls into an O, it has gone too far.
p48: Drain the tuna very well and flake it.
Mix with egg, breadcrumbs and finely chopped onion.
Shape the cakes and rest them 10 min to firm up.
Fry over medium heat until golden on both sides.
The cold rest is what stops them falling apart in the pan.
p49: Mix the liquid with the salt and rain in the flour.
Knead until smooth and rest 5 min so it hydrates.
Shape even discs about 1 cm thick.
Griddle in a hot pan until golden on both sides.
If the dough cracks as you shape it, it needs more liquid. It should feel like soft modelling clay.
p50: Mix the dry ingredients on one side and the wet on the other.
Bring them together with the least stirring possible: lumps are fine.
Cook in a pan over medium heat; flip when bubbles appear.
Under-mixing is the whole trick. Beat it smooth and you develop gluten and they turn rubbery.
p51: Blend all the ingredients until very smooth.
Rest the batter at least 20 minutes in the fridge.
Pour a little batter into a hot pan and swirl to coat.
Cook 1 minute a side; the first one almost always fails.
The rest relaxes the gluten, which is why the crêpe comes out thin and flexible instead of leathery.
p52: Melt the butter over medium heat without colouring it.
Add the flour and cook, stirring, for 2 minutes (this is the roux).
Pour in the warm milk little by little, whisking without stopping.
Cook until it thickens and season.
Warm milk and a little at a time: cold and all at once makes lumps that never come out.
p53: Soften the onion in the oil until translucent.
Add the garlic and cook 1 minute more.
Stir in the tomato, the salt and the sugar.
Simmer gently until concentrated and darkened.
Freeze it in portions: it is the base for pastas, pizzas, braises and huevos rancheros.
p54: Put the whole egg, lime, mustard and salt in the jug.
Pour the oil on top and let it settle for 30 seconds.
Blend with the stick blender at the bottom, without moving it, until it emulsifies.
Raise the blender slowly to take in all the oil.
Everything at room temperature. If the egg is cold, the emulsion splits.
p55: Mash very ripe bananas with a fork.
Beat the butter with the sugar, then the eggs.
Fold in the banana and lastly the flour with the baking powder.
Bake at 180°C until a skewer comes out clean.
The blacker the banana, the better the cake. Green ones bring neither sweetness nor aroma.
p56: Melt the chocolate with the butter over a water bath.
Beat the eggs with the sugar until pale and foamy.
Fold in the warm chocolate, then the flour, gently.
Bake at 180°C; pull it out while the centre still wobbles.
Take it out before it looks done: a brownie sets outside the oven and that is what keeps it fudgy.
p57: Put them in the pot with water, sugar, lime and cinnamon.
Cook covered over low heat until they break down.
Crush for a rustic texture or blend for a smooth one.
The lime keeps the colour pale and balances the sweetness.
p63: Beat the eggs with the salt until smooth.
Melt the butter over LOW heat, never medium.
Pour in the egg and stir constantly with a spatula, scraping the base.
Pull them off while they still look glossy and loose.
Low heat and constant movement: the egg sets in tiny curds and comes out creamy, not rubbery.
p64: Heat the oil properly; it should shimmer and move quickly.
Crack the egg close to the surface so it does not splash.
Spoon the hot oil over the white.
Lift it out when the edge is golden and the yolk still runny.
Spooning hot oil over the white sets it from above without ever turning the egg.
p65: Lower the eggs into water that is already boiling, not cold.
Cook 7 min for a creamy yolk, 10 for firm.
Move them straight into iced water.
Going into boiling water shrinks the white away from the shell: that is why they peel cleanly.
p66: Beat egg, milk, sugar and cinnamon in a shallow dish.
Soak each slice 10 seconds a side, without drowning it.
Brown in butter over medium heat.
Over-soaking leaves the centre raw and soggy. Ten seconds a side is plenty.
p67: Bring the milk and salt to a gentle boil.
Add the oats and lower the heat.
Sweeten off the heat and crown with fruit.
The pinch of salt does not make it salty: it makes the sweetness and the grain come through more.
p68: Butter the OUTSIDE of each slice, not the inside.
Build the sandwich with the cheese in the middle.
Cook over medium-low heat, pressing with a spatula.
Flip and brown the other side until the cheese runs.
Medium-low heat: turn it up and the bread burns before the cheese melts.
p69: Mix warm water with salt and rain in the flour.
Knead and rest 5 min so it hydrates.
Shape discs, put cheese in the centre and seal the edge closed.
Griddle in a hot pan until golden on both sides.
Seal the edge properly by turning the disc between your palms, or the cheese escapes in the heat.
p70: Soften the spring onion in the oil.
Add yesterday's rice and toss it loose.
Fold in the beans with a little of their liquid.
Serve with a fried egg on top.
It is a leftovers dish and that is the point: yesterday's rice stays loose and takes flavour better.
p71: Put the banana, milk and sugar in the blender.
Add the ice and blend again.
Use a properly ripe banana: a green one is astringent and you end up doubling the sugar.
p72: Roll the oranges under your palm on the counter before cutting them.
Sweeten only if it needs it.
Serve at once, before the aroma fades.
Rolling the orange bursts the vesicles inside and yields a great deal more juice.
p73: Squeeze the limes; do not blend the peel.
Mix the juice with the water and sugar until dissolved.
Taste and adjust: it should be tart, not sweet.
Blend the whole lime and it turns bitter within minutes, from the oil in the peel.
p74: Heat the milk without letting it boil.
Add the chocolate in pieces and stir until dissolved.
Serve with cheese alongside to dip in.
The pinch of salt deepens the cocoa: it is the trick that separates good hot chocolate from flat.
p75: Boil the water with the panela until dissolved.
Take it off the heat and add the ground coffee.
Cover and let it steep for 3 minutes.
Never boil coffee: water off the heat pulls out aroma without pulling out bitterness.
p76: Beat the egg with the milk and salt in a large mug.
Cook 40 seconds and take it out to stir.
Add the cheese and cook another 30 seconds.
Rest 1 minute: it finishes setting on its own.
Use a mug twice the volume you think you need: the egg climbs enormously and overflows.
p77: Prick the potato several times with a fork.
Cook 5 minutes, turn and cook 4 more.
Check it gives when squeezed; if not, 2 minutes more.
Open it in a cross, fluff the inside and season.
Pricking lets the steam out. Without it, the potato bursts inside the microwave.
p78: Cut everything the same size and put it in a deep dish.
Add the water and cover, leaving one corner open.
Cook 4 minutes; check they are still firm.
Drain and season with butter and lime.
The open corner lets pressure escape; sealed completely, the dish jumps.
p79: Cut into even batons and leave them 10 min in cold water.
Dry them VERY well and toss with the oil.
Cook at 200°C in a single layer, shaking halfway.
Season the moment they come out, while hot.
The soak pulls out starch and the drying removes water: those two things are what make them crisp.
p80: Pat the chicken dry with paper and marinate it.
Arrange skin side up, without overlapping.
Turn and finish 8 minutes more at 200°C.
No overlapping and skin up: the air has to circulate or it steams instead of crisping.
p81: Peel and cut into thick diagonal slices.
They should be golden at the edges and soft inside.
With no frying oil the plantain's sugar caramelizes on its own. They come out sweeter than fried.
p82: Cut everything into large, even pieces.
Toss with oil and salt until coated.
Look for dark edges: that is where the flavour is.
Large pieces: small ones dry out before they brown in the hot air.
p83: Take the meat out of the fridge 30 min ahead and marinate it.
Heat the grill until you cannot hold a hand near it.
Sear 4 minutes a side without moving it.
The rest is not optional: cut it straight away and all the juice ends up on the board.
p84: Boil the potatoes until almost tender.
Put them on the grill with the chorizos.
Turn the chorizo often so it does not burst.
Serve with lime and chilli sauce.
Par-boiling the potato is what stops it burning outside while still raw inside.
p85: Strip the husk and silk from the cob.
Brush it with butter while hot.
Finish with salt and grated cheese.
Turning often toasts it evenly. Left still, it burns on one side and stays raw on the other.
